source.title: 'Spray and pray': How AI job applications can backfire
source.summary: Graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, research suggests. But some say their peer group has no choice.
source.evidence_text:
We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates , external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.
According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.
On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.
And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.
Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.
While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.
"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."
Graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, research suggests. But some say their peer group has no choice.
He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.
He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates .
However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.
"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."
It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.
While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.
"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."
This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".
EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.
She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

lesson.title: Using Technology for Job Applications

options: People who are trying to get a job.
Companies that are looking for new workers.
Computer programs that write letters.

quiz.question: What do employers still want to see from each person?
options: Their real personality.
Their fast typing speed.
Their expensive computer equipment.
option_feedback: Yes. Employers want to see who the person really is.
The story does not mention typing speed.
The text does not say employers care about expensive equipment.

grammar.explanation: We use the present continuous tense (a form of "be" + verb-ing) to describe situations that are currently changing or developing over time. In this reading, the phrase "are increasingly using" shows a growing trend among people looking for jobs.

quiz.question: Why are employers changing their hiring processes?

quiz.question: What does it mean if a process is "exhausting"?
options: It makes you feel extremely tired.
It is very fast and efficient.

option_feedback: "Exhausting" means causing extreme physical or mental tiredness.
An exhausting process is tiring, not necessarily fast or efficient.
An exhausting process drains your energy; it does not give you more.

options: They ask people not to use artificial intelligence while using it themselves.

Misconduct is a human behavioural issue, not a computer error.
Misconduct refers to bad behaviour, not an online communication method.

lesson.title: How AI is Disrupting Graduate Job Applications
lesson.overview: As graduates increasingly rely on artificial intelligence to navigate a saturated job market, employers face the delicate challenge of maintaining fair and authentic recruitment processes.

vocabulary.definition: To alter facts or information in a way that creates a misleading or inaccurate impression.
Happening, existing, or done at exactly the same time.
So full or crowded with people or things that no more can be added or accommodated.
To make something as effective, perfect, or functional as possible.
Specific technical terms or fashionable phrases that are popular in a particular context or required by algorithms.
A precarious situation requiring careful balancing between two contrasting choices or dangers.
Strict, unbending, and unable to be changed or adapted to different circumstances.
Occurring before or serving as preparation for the main or final part of a process.
Before the natural, expected, or scheduled time; too early.
An illogical or unfair difference or inconsistency between two or more things.

grammar.explanation: The conjunction "while" can be followed directly by an active present participle ("-ing" form) to contrast two concurrent actions or requirements. This advanced structure gracefully omits the subject and auxiliary verb, keeping the sentence concise and polished.
grammar.example_quote: This creates a delicate tightrope for applicants, who must sound human while still satisfying the rigid parameters of algorithmic filters.

quiz.question: Based on the reading, what is the primary consequence of the "spray and pray" method?
options: It artificially intensifies competition in the job market.
It guarantees that employers will overlook qualified candidates.
It forces companies to stop using automated screening.
option_feedback: Correct. The text notes that "spray and pray" tactics generate multiple simultaneous submissions, which intensifies competition.
Incorrect. While high volume makes screening harder, the text does not claim it guarantees qualified applicants are overlooked.
Incorrect. Employers are actually relying more on automated screening to manage the massive volume of applications.

quiz.question: What does "distort" mean in the context of the first sentence?
options: To present information in a misleading or inaccurate way.
To completely fabricate a false work history.
To mistakenly submit the wrong qualifications.
option_feedback: Correct. "Distort" means to alter or twist facts to give a misleading impression of one's qualifications.
Incorrect. "Distorting" implies embellishing or twisting existing facts, whereas fabricating means entirely inventing something untrue.
Incorrect. Distorting is a deliberate attempt to appear better suited for a role, not an accidental submission error.

quiz.question: Why does the text describe the application process as a "tightrope"?
options: Applicants must balance sounding natural with including specific phrases for AI filters.
Jobseekers are forced to complete assessments under strict algorithmic time limits.
Employers are unsure whether to hire human workers or automate roles entirely.
option_feedback: Correct. The "tightrope" refers to the delicate balance of sounding authentically human while using necessary buzzwords.
Incorrect. The difficulty lies in satisfying algorithmic content filters, not managing strict time limits.
Incorrect. The tightrope metaphor describes the applicants' struggle with AI tools, not a dilemma over automating human jobs.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the best synonym for "rigid" as used to describe algorithmic filters?
options: Inflexible.
Unnecessarily complicated.
Fundamentally flawed.
option_feedback: Correct. "Rigid" describes something strict or unbending, such as the strict criteria used by algorithmic filters.
Incorrect. While the filters may be complex, "rigid" specifically refers to their inflexibility.
Incorrect. "Rigid" means strict; it does not suggest that the technology is broken or defective.

quiz.question: What "unethical practice" did 92% of surveyed employers suspect?
options: Candidates relying on real-time generative assistants during online interviews.
Applicants submitting cover letters that were completely written by AI.
Recruiters using algorithms to automatically reject diverse candidates.
option_feedback: Correct. The reading explicitly states that 92% of employers suspected individuals of using real-time generative assistants during video interviews.
Incorrect. Using AI for preliminary stages like cover letters is increasingly tolerated, not cited as the primary unethical practice.
Incorrect. The "unethical practices" refers to the actions of the applicants, not the automated screening by recruiters.

quiz.question: In the phrase "while still satisfying the rigid parameters", what grammatical structure is used to create a concise contrast?
options: A conjunction followed immediately by a present participle.
A preposition paired with a passive infinitive verb.
A relative pronoun introducing a non-defining clause.
option_feedback: Correct. The conjunction "while" connects directly to the present participle "satisfying," creating a concise contrast.
Incorrect. "Satisfying" is an active present participle, not an infinitive verb.
Incorrect. "While" is a conjunction of time or contrast, not a relative pronoun like "who" or "which".

quiz.question: In the phrase "prematurely close its graduate scheme", what does "prematurely" mean?
options: Before the expected or scheduled time.
Without giving applicants any prior warning.
Due to a sudden lack of available funding.
option_feedback: Correct. Closing a scheme "prematurely" means ending it earlier than was originally planned.
Incorrect. While they may not have given warning, "prematurely" refers to the timing being early, not the lack of notice.
Incorrect. The scheme closed early because of an overwhelming influx of applications, not a funding shortage.

quiz.question: Why did EDF delay its document reviews and focus on behaviour-based assessments?
options: To create an assessment environment that is harder to manipulate using AI.
To reduce the overall number of applications they receive in the future.
To save money on human recruitment staff during preliminary stages.
option_feedback: Correct. EDF is prioritising behaviour-based assessments to make their hiring procedures robust against AI manipulation.
Incorrect. Changing the assessment format does not prevent individuals from applying or reduce the initial volume.
Incorrect. The shift aims to ensure a fair, AI-proof evaluation, not to cut financial costs on recruiters.

quiz.question: What does a "discrepancy" refer to in the context of the reading?
options: An imbalance where some applicants use AI extensively and others do not.
A technical error within the automated recruitment software.
A disagreement between recruiters about which candidate to hire.
option_feedback: Correct. A "discrepancy" is a lack of consistency; here, it refers to the uneven adoption of AI that destroys a level playing field.
Incorrect. The discrepancy describes human behavioural differences, not a glitch in the software itself.
Incorrect. It refers to a difference in applicant methods, not an argument among the recruitment staff.

quiz.question: How do major UK employers generally feel about AI in recruitment?
options: They are growing tolerant of AI for early stages but object to its use during live interviews.
They universally ban any AI assistance to maintain a completely level playing field.
They encourage the use of AI in interviews to evaluate applicants' technical skills.
option_feedback: Correct. The survey shows employers are tolerant of AI during preliminary phases but view real-time assistance as unethical practices.
Incorrect. The text states they are actually growing more tolerant of AI use during preliminary stages.
